reference.source: U.S. Naval Air Station Patuxent River, 'Performance Test Each 1000th Airplane' (TED No. PTR-2125), 7 Sep 1944, F6F-5 BuNo 58310, Overload Fighter loading, military-power trial data as tabulated at wwiiaircraftperformance.org/f6f/f6f.html (summary table re-read 2026-09-12). That table states 'Gross weight -lbs 12,420' for this airplane, which is testMassKg = 5633.62 kg -- so the trial weight is stated and no substitution of a published normal-loaded weight was needed. topSpeedMps = 391.0 mph at an airplane critical altitude of 23,100 ft; climbRateMps = 2,660 ft/min at sea level. stallSpeedMps = 98.0 mph, the table's CLEAN, POWER-OFF stall: the flight model has no flaps or landing gear, so the clean figure is the like-for-like one. The same table's landing-condition power-off stall is 84.5 mph (37.77 m/s), which an earlier revision of this file cited by mistake -- it is unreachable for a model with no high-lift devices. Weights and dimensions cross-checked against the Grumman F6F Hellcat Wikipedia infobox (334 sq ft / 31.0 sq m wing, 42 ft 10 in / 13.06 m span, 9,238 lb / 4,190 kg empty). rollRateDegPerSec is NOT corroborated by this source and remains an unsourced estimate. takeoffDistanceM is the SAME table's 'Take-off distance, no wind' row: 755 ft = 230.124 m, FULL FLAPS, take-off speed 86.5 mph, 2700 RPM -- the table's other take-off figure, 335 ft in a 25-knot wind, is not used because the model carries no wind (Ruling R29). This is NOT a like-for-like figure: the model has no flaps, no rolling friction and no ground effect, all of which push a simulated roll shorter than a full-flaps trial roll, so the take-off card compares against it at a wider, honestly-justified tolerance -- see tools/testcards/measure.ts and f6f.test.ts. windmillCd0 = 0.0422 is an ENGINEERING ESTIMATE, not a trial figure, and is labeled as one here for the same reason rollRateDegPerSec is: no wind-tunnel or flight-test figure for a windmilling R-2800 disc on this airframe was located. It is 2.00x the clean cd0 of 0.0211 -- a windmilling constant-speed propeller roughly doubles clean parasitic drag -- taken as the MIDDLE of the published 1x-3x range for a stopped or windmilling propeller, which spans that much depending on blade pitch. Measured on this airplane 2026-09-16, level at 50 ft with altitude pinned so drag is the only loss, 250 mph bleeding to 100 mph: 79.3 s / 6.01 km with no propeller drag at all (the state Mark flew and reported as unrealistic), 50.5 s at 1x, 37.5 s / 2.70 km at this value, 30.0 s at 3x. Expect to tune it once someone flies a dead-stick approach.
